Body corporate and strata exterior cleaning in Melbourne

Common property: everyone's, therefore nobody's

The shared driveway, the path to the bins, the entry glazing, the letterbox surround and the car park nobody owns individually. Quoted as one scope so a committee can approve a figure, invoiced once, and recorded per attendance for the minutes.

  • One scope, one invoice, one contact
  • Priced per visit for an annual budget
  • Attendance recorded for the committee
Get A Quote 0400 638 010
  1. Home
  2. Commercial
  3. Body corporate and strata

The actual problem is approval, not cleaning

Common property degrades slowly and nobody owns the decision to do something about it. By the time it is bad enough that somebody raises it at a meeting, it has been bad for two years and it is now a restoration job rather than a maintenance one.

Then the approval cycle starts: three quotes, a meeting, a resolution, a scheduling conversation. The cleaning takes a day. The process takes a quarter. Which is why common property work is quoted as a scope and a frequency approved once, rather than as a job approved every time, and why the per-visit figure matters more to a committee than the hourly rate ever will.

Common property inventory

What is usually in scope, and what is usually forgotten

Worth running through this before the next budget rather than after the next complaint.

The surfaces that make up most common property exterior scopes in Melbourne, with a realistic frequency.
  Why it matters Typical frequency
Shared driveway and car park The largest surface and the one every resident and visitor drives on Twice yearly, more where there are trees
Pedestrian paths and stairs Slip risk first, appearance second. Shaded paths go green fast Twice yearly
Bin enclosure and surrounds The single most complained about area in most complexes Quarterly, and worth more than it costs
Entry glazing and lobby doors First impression for every visitor and prospective buyer Monthly to quarterly
Letterbox bank and surround Everyone touches it, nobody cleans it Twice yearly
Common walls and render Mould on the shaded elevation of a complex reads as neglect across the whole property Every two years
Visitor parking and line marking Oil, tyre marks and biological growth. Usually overlooked entirely Annually
Gutters on common buildings A blocked box gutter on a shared roof is a far more expensive failure than a house one Annually, twice under trees

How we work with committees and managers

Four things that make it easier

A scope you can put in a motion

Written as a list of surfaces with a frequency and a per-visit figure, so it can be read at a meeting and voted on without anyone having to interpret it.

Approved once, then it happens

The whole point. A twelve month schedule approved at one meeting rather than four separate approvals through the year.

One contact, whoever that is

A strata manager, a committee chair or a building manager. We deal with one person and do not chase residents.

A record of every attendance

Date, scope and condition, so there is something in the file when a resident asks what the levy paid for.

Works for self-managed buildings too

A lot of smaller complexes in Melbourne are self managed, which usually means one owner doing it in their own time. A standing arrangement is worth more there than anywhere, because it removes the job of organising it. Same scope, same per-visit pricing, invoiced to whoever handles the account.

Questions

From committees and strata managers

Can you quote in a format we can take to a meeting?

Yes, and that is how we write it. A list of surfaces, a frequency against each, a per-visit figure and an annual total, so a committee can read it and resolve on it without anyone having to interpret a trade quote.

If your manager has a preferred format, send it and we will use theirs.

Do we have to get three quotes?

Most owners corporations do under their own rules, and that is entirely reasonable. What is worth doing is making sure the three quotes are for the same scope, because exterior cleaning quotes vary enormously in what they include.

Ask specifically whether each one covers the bin area, the letterbox surround and visitor parking. Those three are the usual difference between a cheap quote and a complete one.

How do you handle access to the complex?

However your building already works: a fob, a code, a building manager or a key safe. It is agreed before the first visit rather than sorted out at the gate.

Most of the work is on open common property and needs no access at all beyond the driveway.

Will residents be disrupted?

Some, briefly. A shared driveway has to be worked in sections so residents can get in and out, and that takes longer than closing it would. We give notice of the day so cars can be moved.

Where a complex can genuinely close an area, say a visitor car park on a Sunday morning, it is faster and cheaper, and we will tell you if that is worth organising.

Who pays if a resident damages something after you have cleaned?

Nobody, in the sense that it is not a defect. We photograph condition on attendance, which means there is a record of what the surface looked like when we left. That has settled a few disagreements.

Can you deal with graffiti when it happens?

Yes, as a call out, and for complexes that get tagged it is worth being part of the standing arrangement rather than a new approval each time. Delay is what makes graffiti harder to remove, and an approval cycle is exactly that delay.

For repeat targets, anti graffiti coating changes the cost of every future incident.
